Distinguish structural and incidental missingness in a Solomon design

Source: R/solomon_validate.R
check_solomon_missing.Rd

Classifies missing values in Solomon design data and explains the supported response to each kind. Pretest scores are structurally absent for participants assigned to the unpretested groups: withholding the pretest is the experimental manipulation (Solomon, 1949), so those values must never be imputed. Other missing values are incidental and are handled according to the missing-data literature (Rubin, 1976; Little & Rubin, 2019).

Usage

check_solomon_missing(
  y_post,
  treat,
  pretested,
  y_pre = NULL,
  control = NULL,
  data = NULL,
  covariates = NULL
)

Arguments

y_post

Numeric posttest scores.

treat

Treatment indicator coded 0/1 (or logical); or a factor or character vector of conditions, with the control named by control.

pretested

Pretest indicator coded 0/1 (or logical).

y_pre

Optional numeric pretest scores, missing by design for unpretested participants.

control

The control condition when treat is a factor or character vector with more than two conditions, a Solomon N-group design; see fit_solomon_glm(). With two conditions the result is the same as with a 0/1 treat.

data

Optional data frame. When supplied, the other data arguments are looked up in it first, as bare column names (y_post = post) or as strings (y_post = "post").

covariates

Optional covariates recorded in all groups, such as gender: a data frame, or, with data, the names of its columns. They enter the fit behind the gap and the delta line, and loss is shown by each of them (see "Missing posttests and the pretest effects").

Value

An object of class solomon_missing, a list with:

  • by_cell: the counts in each Solomon cell, in the columns group, cell, pretested, treat, n, posttest_missing, pretest_structural, pretest_incidental, and pretest_unexpected.

  • counts: the totals by category.

  • pattern: "none", "structural", "incidental", or "mixed".

  • guidance: for each category present, its count, the interpretation, the supported response, and the sources (category, n, interpretation, response, and sources).

  • pretest_supplied: whether pretest scores were supplied.

The checks of missing posttests for the pretest effects (see "Missing posttests and the pretest effects"), the elements that need a pretest being NULL without a numeric y_pre:

  • attrition: groups, each group's condition, pretested, n, posttest_missing, and share; overall, the share missing; by_pretest, the shares of the pretested and the unpretested; pretest_difference, the first minus the second; by_condition, the share missing in each condition; condition_difference, the largest difference between conditions; p.value, Fisher's exact test of loss by pretest condition; and differ, whether it is below .05.

  • pretest_scores: for each pretested condition, n participants with a pretest and their mean pretest mean_all; n_with and mean_with for those with a posttest; n_without and mean_without for those without; difference (without minus with); shift (with minus all); and shift_se, its standard error.

  • selection_test: the Wald test of equal shifts, its statistic (chi-square), df, and p.value; and selection_differ, whether the p-value is below .05.

  • gap: slope, m1, the mean pretest of the pretested participants analyzed and not_analyzed, the gap between the centers, and predicted, what the pretested dropouts' pretests predict for them.

  • unpretested: for each unpretested group, condition, n, posttest_missing, m0, and delta, the offset the default assumes.

  • covariates: one table for each covariate: by pretest condition and level, n, posttest_missing, share, analyzed_share, p.value, and test ("exact" or "simulated"); or, for a numeric covariate with more than two values, its mean among those with (mean_with) and without (mean_without) a posttest. NULL without covariates.

  • missing_pretest: for each pretested condition, the participants with a posttest and no pretest (n_without_pretest, mean_without_pretest, their mean posttest) and those with both scores (n_with_pretest, mean_with_pretest).

  • raw_pretest_effects: the pretest effects of a fit without the pretest, in the columns of an effects table, when the selection differs or a pretested participant lacks a pretest; otherwise NULL.

  • unverifiable: whether any unpretested posttest is missing.

For a design with several treatments, by_cell has one row for each of the 2(k + 1) groups, its treat column holds the condition, and conditions names the control and the treatments.

Details

Categories:

  • Structural pretest absence: unpretested participants have no pretest. Unlike planned missing-data designs, in which unmeasured values exist and can be imputed (Graham et al., 2006), an imputed pretest here would describe a measurement that never occurred.

  • Incidental pretest missingness: pretested participants without a pretest score. solomonR analyses currently use complete cases and warn. Because treatment is randomized, deterministic mean imputation of the pretest (without using treatment or outcome), with a missingness indicator when pretests may not be missing completely at random, retains these participants without biasing the treatment effect (White & Thompson, 2005; Groenwold et al., 2012). This concerns the treatment effect only: every fit with the pretest as a covariate drops these participants from the pretest effects, at either pretest center, and when their loss relates to baseline those effects are biased while a fit without the pretest is not (issue #142).

  • Incidental posttest missingness: missing outcomes. For the treatment contrasts, complete-case analysis is unbiased when missingness is unrelated to the outcome given the variables in the model (Little & Rubin, 2019); attrition that differs across the groups should be reported. The pretest effects also depend on the mean pretest at which the pretested groups are compared; see "Missing posttests and the pretest effects" below.

  • Unexpected pretest scores: pretest values recorded for unpretested participants, which usually indicate a coding or assignment error. They are ignored by solomonR analyses.

  • Unassigned participants: missing treatment or pretest assignment.

Pretest categories are NA when y_pre is not supplied.

Designs with several treatments: give treat as a factor or character vector of conditions and name the control with control. The counts are then given for each of the 2(k + 1) groups of a design with k treatments (Steyn, 2009): each treatment and the control, with and without a pretest.

Not supported: this function does not test the missingness mechanism, perform imputation, or provide sensitivity analyses for outcome missingness that depends on unobserved values.

Missing posttests and the pretest effects

With a pretest covariate, the pretest effects compare the pretested groups, at a mean pretest, with the unpretested groups, and when posttests are missing that mean can be taken over the pretested participants analyzed (the default of fit_solomon_glm()) or over every observed pretest (pretest_center = "observed"); see "The pretest effect when posttests are missing" in fit_solomon_glm(). The data cannot tell which is right. The result gives the checks of the decision record on issue #135 (section 5), and the print method summarizes them:

  1. Posttests missing by group: the overall rate, and the differential attrition between the pretest conditions and between the conditions (What Works Clearinghouse, 2022, p. 40). Equal rates do not show that the same kinds of participants were lost (Campbell & Stanley, 1963/1966, pp. 15–16). When Fisher's exact test of loss by pretest condition gives p < .05, the print says that the loss rates differ, which suggests that taking the pretest changed attrition, so that neither center is assured. That rule is the package's: no source fixes one for the pretest conditions.

  2. Pretest scores of those lost: for each pretested group, the mean pretest of the participants with and without a posttest (Campbell, 1957, pp. 301–302; Campbell & Stanley, 1963/1966, pp. 15–16).

  3. Selection by condition: each pretested condition's selection shift, the mean pretest of those with a posttest minus that of every participant with a pretest, with its standard error from the shift's influence function (Stefanski & Boos, 2002), and a Wald chi-square test of equal shifts across the conditions. A condition that lost no posttest has a shift of exactly 0. When the test gives p < .05 (the package's rule; no source fixes one), the conditions may have lost different kinds of participants. Neither center then gives both conditional pretest effects: in the decision record's case S3 (losses by baseline in the control arms and at random in the treated arms, alike in both pretest conditions) the default misstated both, although not their average when the pretested groups kept equal numbers, and the observed center misstated one of them and their average. Pretest x Treatment is biased at every center (issue #143). The pretest effects of a fit without the pretest, the raw comparison of posttest means in each condition, are then given. The test does not depend on the units of the pretest. When every group loses by the same rule it rejects at about its nominal rate: in a check on issue #135 (1,000 data sets for each setting; part 8 of tools/pretest-center-check.R in the package's source), in 5.7% of data sets with 200 participants per group and 4.4% with 50 when loss depended on baseline, and in 5.8% and 4.5% when it was completely at random.

  4. The gap between the centers: the pretest effects at the analyzed center minus those at the observed center, b m1 (completers' minus dropouts' mean pretest), with b the pretest slope and m1 the share of pretested participants with a pretest who are not analyzed, from a fit on the identity link with covariates. This is the adjustment of What Works Clearinghouse (2022, Equation H.2, p. 207).

  5. The unpretested groups: for each, its share without a posttest, m0, and the offset the default assumes for its dropouts, the delta line of fit_solomon_glm(). A group that lost no posttests is named: if the data hold everyone randomized to it, the default's pretest effect in that condition is right only if the pretested groups' losses, taken together, were unrelated to baseline, because the default's center pools the pretested groups.

  6. Covariates recorded in all groups (covariates): loss by covariate within each pretest condition, and the covariate's distribution among the participants with a posttest (Lee, 2005, Remark 4, p. 16; Groenwold et al., 2014). For a covariate with levels, loss by level is tested with Fisher's exact test when there are two levels, and with a p-value simulated from 10,000 tables with the same margins, under a fixed seed, when there are more, because the exact test of a larger table can exceed its workspace at ordinary sample sizes; that choice is the package's, and no source fixes one. Dukes et al. (1995, p. 413) compared the course grades of the students lost in this way. A covariate that predicts the posttest belongs in the model; that it weakens both centers' assumptions is the record's inference, not a checked result.

  7. Pretested participants with a posttest and no pretest: their number and mean posttest beside those of the pretested participants with both scores, and the raw comparison, which keeps them (issue #142).

  8. What cannot be checked: the unpretested groups' losses cannot be checked against baseline (Campbell, 1957, p. 305). When only those groups lost posttests, the two centers coincide, but neither is protected; only the delta line reaches that case. If an unpretested group's dropouts would have scored Delta above its completers, the pretest effect in its condition is m0 Delta lower, m0 being that group's share without a posttest (see "The pretest effect when posttests are missing" in fit_solomon_glm()).

The checks on the pretest (items 2 to 5 and 7) need numeric pretest scores and are left out otherwise. validate_solomon() leaves out all of them.

See also

validate_solomon()

Examples

data(solomon_example)

# Structural absence only: pretests are absent by design in Groups 3 and 4.
with(solomon_example, check_solomon_missing(y_post, treat, pretested, y_pre))
#> Solomon missingness check
#> Pattern: structural pretest absence only (expected in a Solomon design)
#> 
#>  Group                   Cell  n Post missing Pre absent (design) Pre missing
#>      1   Pretested, treatment 30            0                   0           0
#>      2     Pretested, control 30            0                   0           0
#>      3 Unpretested, treatment 30            0                  30           0
#>      4   Unpretested, control 30            0                  30           0
#>  Pre unexpected
#>               0
#>               0
#>               0
#>               0
#> 
#> Structural pretest absence (n = 60)
#>   Participants assigned to the unpretested groups were never pretested; the
#>   absence of a pretest is the experimental manipulation.
#>   Response: Do not impute. Use analyses that respect the design, such as
#>     fit_solomon_glm(), fit_solomon_ml(), fit_solomon_classic(), or SEM.
#>     Unlike planned missing-data designs, where unmeasured values exist and
#>     can be imputed, an imputed pretest here would describe a measurement that
#>     never occurred.
#>   Sources: Solomon (1949); Graham et al. (2006)

# Mixed: add a lost pretest and a missing posttest.
d <- solomon_example
d$y_pre[which(d$pretested == 1)[1]] <- NA
d$y_post[which(d$pretested == 0)[1]] <- NA
with(d, check_solomon_missing(y_post, treat, pretested, y_pre))
#> Solomon missingness check
#> Pattern: structural pretest absence and incidental missingness
#> 
#>  Group                   Cell  n Post missing Pre absent (design) Pre missing
#>      1   Pretested, treatment 30            0                   0           1
#>      2     Pretested, control 30            0                   0           0
#>      3 Unpretested, treatment 30            1                  30           0
#>      4   Unpretested, control 30            0                  30           0
#>  Pre unexpected
#>               0
#>               0
#>               0
#>               0
#> 
#> Structural pretest absence (n = 60)
#>   Participants assigned to the unpretested groups were never pretested; the
#>   absence of a pretest is the experimental manipulation.
#>   Response: Do not impute. Use analyses that respect the design, such as
#>     fit_solomon_glm(), fit_solomon_ml(), fit_solomon_classic(), or SEM.
#>     Unlike planned missing-data designs, where unmeasured values exist and
#>     can be imputed, an imputed pretest here would describe a measurement that
#>     never occurred.
#>   Sources: Solomon (1949); Graham et al. (2006)
#> 
#> Incidental pretest missingness (n = 1)
#>   Participants assigned to be pretested have no pretest score. Determine
#>   whether the pretest was administered but the score was lost, or never
#>   administered, which is a departure from the assigned pretest condition.
#>   Response: solomonR analyses currently use complete cases and warn. Because
#>     treatment is randomized, deterministic mean imputation of the pretest
#>     (without using treatment or outcome), with a missingness indicator when
#>     pretests may not be missing completely at random, retains these
#>     participants without biasing the treatment effect. That holds for the
#>     treatment effect only: the pretest effects of a fit with the pretest drop
#>     these participants at either pretest center, and are biased when their
#>     loss relates to baseline (issue #142). If the pretest was never
#>     administered, report the departure and analyze participants as assigned.
#>   Sources: White & Thompson (2005); Groenwold et al. (2012)
#> 
#> Incidental posttest missingness (n = 1)
#>   Posttest scores are missing, so these participants are excluded from
#>   complete-case analyses.
#>   Response: For the treatment contrasts, complete-case analysis is unbiased
#>     when missingness is unrelated to the outcome given the variables in the
#>     model. The pretest effects also depend on the mean pretest at which they
#>     are evaluated; see `pretest_center` in fit_solomon_glm() and the
#>     diagnostics below. Report missingness by cell, because attrition that
#>     differs across the four groups can undermine the randomized comparisons,
#>     and consider sensitivity analyses if missingness may depend on the
#>     unobserved outcome.
#>   Sources: Rubin (1976); Little & Rubin (2019)
#> 
#> Missing posttests and the pretest effects (see ?fit_solomon_glm)
#>   Posttests missing: 0.8% overall; pretested 0.0%, unpretested 1.7% (a
#>   difference of -1.7 points; Fisher's exact test, p = 1.000); by condition,
#>   control 0.0% and treatment 1.7% (the largest difference 1.7 points).
#>   Equal loss rates do not show that the same kinds of participants were lost.
#>   Pretested participants with a posttest and no pretest: 1. Their mean posttest
#>   was 60.00, against 55.29 for the pretested participants with both scores.
#>   Every fit with the pretest drops them, at either center (issue #142); the raw
#>   comparison below keeps them.
#>   Raw comparison (a fit without the pretest, HC3; 95% CI):
#>     Pretest effect | control   3.40  [-1.36,  8.16]
#>     Pretest effect | treated   0.99  [-4.19,  6.17]
#>     Pretest main effect        2.20  [-1.32,  5.71]
#>   The unpretested groups' losses cannot be checked against baseline (Campbell,
#>   1957, p. 305); with only those groups losing posttests, the two centers
#>   coincide, but neither is protected. Only the delta line reaches that case: if
#>   an unpretested group's dropouts would have scored Delta above its completers,
#>   the pretest effect in its condition is m0 x Delta lower, m0 being that
#>   group's share without a posttest (see ?fit_solomon_glm).

# A six-group design: two treatments and a control (Mai et al., 2020),
# with loss by gender in each pretest condition.
check_solomon_missing(post_behavior, condition, pretested, pre_behavior,
                      control = "Control", data = mai2020, covariates = "gender")

#>   Response: For the treatment contrasts, complete-case analysis is unbiased
